paragraphs: Estimating a sparse Gaussian graphical model usually requires choosing how strongly to regularize the model. That choice can involve expensive cross-validation, even for methods described as tuning-free in an asymptotic sense. This paper proposes an estimator that removes this practical tuning step by using regularization parameters that do not depend on the particular model being estimated.

The method estimates the target precision matrix one column at a time, and its optimization problems can be solved through linear programming. The authors establish minimax optimal convergence rates under several norms: the estimator meets theoretical benchmarks for estimation accuracy measured in different ways. They also introduce a second stage using nonconvex penalties and prove that it has the strong oracle property.

Numerical studies report favorable statistical performance, including robustness when the Gaussian assumption is violated. In the evaluated heavy-tailed settings, the methods substantially outperform competing approaches. The contribution therefore combines a reduction in tuning effort with theoretical accuracy guarantees and empirical evidence that the approach remains useful beyond Gaussian data.
icml-2022-a-completely-tuning-free-and-r.tldr: A tuning-free estimator for sparse precision matrices combines optimal convergence guarantees with strong empirical performance on heavy-tailed data.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods estimate how changing an agent’s policy would change its expected return. The standard theorem requires states to be weighted according to a particular discounted distribution under the target policy. Many practical algorithms use samples that do not follow this distribution, creating a mismatch that can lead learning toward poor solutions.

This paper reconstructs the policy gradient from the start state without prescribing a particular sampling strategy. Its central object is a gradient critic, which represents information needed to calculate that gradient. A new Bellman equation expresses this information recursively, allowing the critic to be learned through temporal-difference updates from a stream of off-policy data.

The authors prove that the resulting estimator is unbiased under specified realizability conditions, regardless of the sampling strategy. Those conditions qualify the guarantee; sampling flexibility alone does not establish unbiasedness. Experiments show a better bias-variance trade-off and improved performance with off-policy samples. The approach makes the gradient itself something that can be learned recursively while addressing the distribution mismatch.
icml-2022-a-temporal-difference-approach.tldr: A recursively learned gradient critic enables model-free policy gradient estimation from off-policy data, with unbiasedness under realizability conditions.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy is often trained specifically for one agent’s physical form. Changing that form can mean training another policy from scratch. Work on transferable control instead asks whether a policy trained across diverse agents with similar objectives can operate an unfamiliar agent immediately. Earlier approaches to this problem relied on manually designed descriptions of each agent’s morphology.

AnyMorph learns a representation of morphology directly through the reinforcement learning objective. The information used to adapt control is therefore learned as part of pursuing the task, rather than supplied as an explicit description of the agent’s body. The authors present this as the first reinforcement learning algorithm to generalize policies to new morphologies without requiring such a description in advance.

On the standard benchmark for agent-agnostic control, the method improves on the reported state of the art for zero-shot transfer to unseen agents. Here, zero-shot transfer means using the learned policy without retraining for the new morphology. The findings support learning morphology representations as a practical route to transferable control.
icml-2022-anymorph-learning-transferable.tldr: AnyMorph learns morphology representations through reinforcement learning to transfer control policies to unfamiliar agents without explicit body descriptions.

paragraphs: An update rule that converges in one kind of game can behave poorly in another. This paper starts from the observation that variants of multiplicative weights have opposite convergence behavior in zero-sum and cooperative games. It asks whether an agent can learn to adjust an optimization rule according to the structure of the game being played.

The proposed framework uses a reinforcement learning policy to choose update coefficients along a trajectory, aiming for the current iterate to converge to a Nash equilibrium. The policy receives a game signature built by decomposing a two-player game into eight components using commuting projection operators. This decomposition provides structured information about the game and unifies several existing game concepts.

The authors also introduce Consensus Multiplicative Weights Update, which extends consensus optimization to constrained settings. It has local convergence guarantees for zero-sum bimatrix games. Experiments show that learned policies exploit game signatures across varied games, while the new update rule performs competitively with fixed coefficients in zero-sum games and learned coefficients across a broader spectrum.
icml-2022-consensus-multiplicative-weigh.tldr: A reinforcement learning policy uses structured game signatures to adapt update rules, alongside a new consensus multiplicative weights algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a Lasso-based classifier behaves when the number of features and the number of examples are of comparable size. That regime matters because neither the data dimension nor the sample count can be treated as small relative to the other. The authors derive a theoretical expression for classification error in terms of the data’s statistical properties.

Their analysis works through the Iterative Soft-Thresholding Algorithm, or ISTA, used in the classification procedure. Studying the iterative algorithm provides a way to explain how Lasso behaves as a classifier and how it differs from competing methods. The authors suggest that this analysis could also be useful beyond classification and might be adapted to related iterative schemes.

The theory additionally supplies a way to optimize the model’s hyperparameters, allowing the costly cross-validation process to be avoided. Applications to synthetic and real data support the theoretical study. Together, these contributions connect predictions about classification error to concrete choices in algorithm design, rather than treating parameter selection and theoretical understanding as separate problems.
icml-2022-deciphering-lasso-based-classi.tldr: A large-dimensional analysis of ISTA explains Lasso classification error and provides theoretical hyperparameter choices that avoid cross-validation.

paragraphs: Design optimization seeks an input, such as a molecule or robot design, that scores highly under an unknown objective. Usually, optimization proceeds by proposing designs and measuring their performance. Those measurements can require physically building and testing candidates, making repeated evaluation expensive and slow. Offline model-based optimization instead seeks good designs using only measurements already available.

This restriction creates algorithmic challenges distinct from those faced by methods that can request new measurements during optimization. Although recent approaches using large neural networks had shown success, inconsistent evaluation made progress difficult to assess. Design-Bench addresses that problem with a shared benchmark, a unified evaluation protocol, and reference implementations of recent methods.

The benchmark contains diverse tasks derived from real optimization problems in biology, materials science, and robotics. Their differing challenges provide a broader basis for assessing offline optimization methods. The paper’s contribution is evaluation infrastructure: shared tasks and implementations make comparisons more consistent and help researchers track progress in learning to design from fixed datasets.
icml-2022-design-bench-benchmarks-for-da.tldr: Design-Bench standardizes evaluation of methods that optimize designs using existing data without collecting new measurements.

paragraphs: Detecting an adversarially perturbed input can appear easier than classifying it correctly. This paper establishes a theoretical connection that challenges that intuition. Given a detector robust to perturbations within distance epsilon, the authors construct a classifier with similar robustness at distance epsilon divided by two. The construction preserves the detector’s data complexity.

The resulting classifier is computationally inefficient, so the reduction is not a practical recipe for building a defense. Its value is diagnostic: a strong detection claim also implies a strong classification claim at the smaller perturbation radius. This gives researchers a way to check whether reported detection performance carries unexpectedly ambitious consequences.

The authors examine 14 published empirical detector defenses. For 12, the claimed results would imply classifiers with robustness far beyond the state of the art, raising doubts about those claims without itself establishing that every claim is false. A reverse reduction also holds: a robust classifier at half the radius yields an inefficient detector at the full radius. Ignoring computational complexity, the problems are therefore nearly equivalent.
icml-2022-detecting-adversarial-examples.tldr: Robust adversarial detection and classification reduce to each other with a factor-of-two radius change when computational efficiency is disregarded.

paragraphs: Deep classifiers often keep training after they classify every training example correctly, further reducing the loss. During this phase, researchers have observed neural collapse: representations within each class gather around their class mean, while different class means form an organized geometric structure aligned with the final layer’s weights. Simplified unconstrained features models have helped explain this behavior.

This paper first studies that simplified model with regularized mean squared error instead of regularized cross-entropy. Its analysis shows that minimizing features can have a more intricate structure than in the cross-entropy setting, with corresponding changes to the weights. The result makes the choice of loss relevant to the geometry predicted by the model.

The authors then add another weight layer and a ReLU nonlinearity, extending their earlier results to this richer model. Experiments demonstrate that the nonlinear extension is useful for modeling neural collapse in practical networks. The work therefore develops a more expressive analytical setting while showing why the simplest geometric description need not capture every loss-dependent structure.
icml-2022-extended-unconstrained-feature.tldr: An extended features model explains richer neural-collapse geometry under mean squared error and incorporates an additional nonlinear layer.

paragraphs: Some theories predict kernel ridge regression through spectral bias: with P training examples, learning preferentially captures target-function components associated with roughly the P largest kernel eigenvalues. These predictions can work well on benchmark data even though their assumptions are not satisfied in practice. This paper investigates where that predictive account succeeds or fails for Laplace kernels.

The authors obtain rigorous results in a one-dimensional model, then use scaling arguments and tests to extend their findings to higher dimensions. One case classifies points according to the sign of their first coordinate, with data density vanishing near the decision boundary according to a positive exponent chi. The analysis connects prediction validity to regularization strength, dimension, and this boundary behavior.

They identify a crossover regularization level scaling as P raised to minus one over d plus chi. Far above it, the replica-method prediction applies; far below it, it does not. Without ridge regularization, spectral bias gives the correct training-curve exponent only as dimension tends to infinity. These findings make the prediction’s validity explicitly dependent on the learning regime.
icml-2022-failure-and-success-of-the-spe.tldr: For the studied Laplace-kernel setting, spectral-bias predictions depend on regularization and dimension, with failures below a derived crossover scale.

paragraphs: Estimating the parameters of an ordinary differential equation means finding dynamics that explain observed behavior from an initial state. This can be a difficult optimization problem. Fenrir uses probabilistic numerics to represent the initial value problem as a Gauss–Markov process whose parameters encode the original dynamics, giving the estimation problem a different mathematical form.

With this construction, estimating differential-equation parameters becomes hyperparameter estimation in a regression model. The authors argue that this transformed problem tends to be considerably easier. The dynamics still shape the model, so the regression formulation incorporates the governing equations rather than treating observations as unrelated samples to be fitted independently.

The paper compares this approach with classical numerical integration and gradient matching. It can handle partial observations, unlike the gradient-matching approach discussed, and offers certain ways to escape local optima that classical integration does not provide. Experiments place its performance on par with or moderately above competing approaches. The reported benefit is a useful reformulation with specific capabilities, rather than uniformly dramatic empirical gains.
icml-2022-fenrir-physics-enhanced-regres.tldr: Fenrir converts differential-equation parameter estimation into Gauss–Markov regression, supporting partial observations and competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Differentially private averaging and clustering can be difficult to use because algorithms are complex or require many observations for accurate results. FriendlyCore is a preprocessing tool intended to make these aggregation tasks easier. It accepts points from an unrestricted metric or pseudometric space, so its formulation does not require a particular coordinate representation.

When the input has effective diameter r, the method produces a stable subset with diameter guaranteed to be r. That subset retains all the points except possibly a few outliers. The construction therefore supplies a controlled collection of points for subsequent private aggregation, potentially simplifying that aggregation or improving its accuracy.

The authors emphasize that FriendlyCore is lightweight and has no dependence on dimension. Experiments show improved accuracy for mean estimation and clustering, including k-means and Gaussian mixture clustering, with performance exceeding tailored methods in the reported evaluations. Its central contribution is a reusable preprocessing step: establishing useful structure in the input can improve multiple private aggregation procedures rather than requiring a separate specialized construction for each task.
icml-2022-friendlycore-practical-differe.tldr: FriendlyCore extracts a stable subset with controlled diameter to simplify or improve differentially private averaging and clustering.

paragraphs: An optimistic reinforcement learning algorithm explores actions whose value could plausibly be high. Bayes-UCBVI implements this idea using an upper quantile of a posterior distribution over Q-values, which describe the value of taking an action in a state. This quantile serves as an upper confidence bound without requiring an elaborate explicit exploration bonus.

The theory covers tabular episodic decision processes whose dynamics can depend on the stage within an episode. The authors prove regret of order the square root of H cubed times S, A, and T, up to logarithmic factors. Here H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T counts episodes. For sufficiently large T, this matches the stated lower bound up to those logarithmic factors.

A new anti-concentration bound for weighted Dirichlet sums is central to the proof. It supports the analysis of posterior-based optimism. The paper also explains an extension beyond tables through a connection to the Bayesian bootstrap. This broader connection is separate from the regret guarantee established for the tabular setting.
icml-2022-from-dirichlet-to-rubin-optimi.tldr: Bayes-UCBVI uses posterior quantiles for optimistic exploration and achieves near-optimal tabular regret without elaborate exploration bonuses.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small weighted selection of data that approximates the full dataset’s fitting loss for every candidate parameter vector. If such a subset exists, an existing optimizer can run on it to obtain an approximate solution to the original problem. This paper studies when that compression is possible for monotonic loss functions.

The first result establishes a barrier: for general monotonic losses, some datasets have no coreset smaller than the full dataset. The authors then show that adding a common regularization term changes the situation. Under an additional natural assumption, satisfied by examples including logistic regression and sigmoid functions, a small coreset exists for any input dataset.

They provide a generic construction taking O(nd + n log n) time, where n is the number of points and d their dimension. Experiments find the resulting coresets effective and substantially smaller than the theoretical bounds predict. The contribution pairs an impossibility result with sufficient conditions for useful compression, clarifying why monotonicity alone cannot guarantee a smaller learning problem.
icml-2022-generic-coreset-for-scalable-l.tldr: Small coresets are impossible for some general monotonic losses, but regularization and an additional assumption enable efficient generic constructions.

paragraphs: Kernel ridge regression and Gaussian processes are widely used for prediction and optimization, but their computational cost can grow cubically with the number of samples. Sparse approximations substantially reduce that burden, reaching linear cost in certain cases. Their empirical usefulness, however, has outpaced the theoretical understanding of the error introduced by approximation.

This paper develops new confidence intervals for two established approaches: the Nyström method and sparse variational Gaussian process approximation. The analysis uses new interpretations of the approximate posterior variance produced by these models. That variance becomes a central tool for reasoning about prediction uncertainty and controlling the consequences of replacing the full kernel model with a cheaper approximation.

The resulting confidence intervals yield improved performance bounds for both regression and optimization. The contribution therefore strengthens the analytical support for existing computational shortcuts rather than introducing sparsity as a new idea. It connects the uncertainty quantities of approximate models to guarantees about their downstream behavior, helping close the gap between practical efficiency and theoretical error analysis.
icml-2022-improved-convergence-rates-for.tldr: New confidence intervals for Nyström and sparse variational Gaussian process methods improve theoretical guarantees for regression and optimization.

paragraphs: Personalized treatment policies choose actions using a patient’s characteristics. Methods can learn such policies from observational data, but policies that perform well may be difficult for clinicians to understand. This paper develops an off-policy learning algorithm whose decisions can be expressed as an OR of AND conditions, making the policy’s rules directly inspectable.

The method searches over hyperboxes to construct these rules. The authors prove a universal approximation theorem: the policy class can approximate any measurable function arbitrarily well. This establishes expressive capacity for the class, rather than asserting that every small rule set achieves that accuracy. To optimize within the class, they combine a tailored column generation procedure with branch-and-bound.

A simulation study reports lower regret than state-of-the-art interpretable off-policy learning methods. Separately, a user study using real clinical data finds that clinical experts rate the learned policies as highly interpretable. These results address both decision quality and human understanding, while the approximation theorem explains why the rule-based representation can support a broad range of policies.
icml-2022-interpretable-off-policy-learn.tldr: Hyperbox search learns expressive treatment policies as readable logical rules, with favorable simulation regret and clinician-rated interpretability.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems minimize a finite sum of component losses. Shuffling gradient methods process those components in an order that can change across passes through the data. This paper introduces Nesterov Accelerated Shuffling Gradient, or NASG, which combines such sampling schemes with Nesterov momentum to improve convergence for convex finite-sum problems.

The authors establish a rate of O(1/T), where T counts epochs, under a unified treatment of shuffling schemes. They report this as an improvement over previous shuffling gradient rates in the convex setting. Their analysis does not require a bounded optimization domain or an assumption that gradients remain bounded, removing two conditions that can constrain convergence arguments.

For randomized shuffling, the convergence bound improves further. The paper also obtains faster convergence near a small neighborhood of the solution when an additional initial condition is satisfied. Numerical simulations demonstrate the algorithm’s efficiency. The results show how momentum and the ordering of component updates can work together, while keeping the stronger local conclusion conditional on the stated initialization requirement.
icml-2022-nesterov-accelerated-shuffling.tldr: NASG combines Nesterov momentum with shuffling to improve convex finite-sum convergence without bounded-domain or bounded-gradient assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper models tensors in which only a small fraction of entries are observed, with that fraction shrinking as the tensor grows. Sparsity here concerns which entries are observed, not a predominance of numerical zeros. The method uses the pattern of observed indices as information alongside the values stored at those indices.

Its representation separates location factors, describing intrinsic properties of tensor nodes, from sociability factors, describing their tendency to interact. Users can choose a trade-off between these types of factors. Hierarchical Gamma processes and Poisson random measures define a generative tensor process with guaranteed asymptotic sparsity. Normalizing that process yields hierarchical Dirichlet processes for sampling observed entry indices.

A Gaussian process then models entry values as nonlinear functions of the factors, capturing complex relationships as well as sparse observation structure. The authors develop stochastic variational inference using finite-partition properties, transformations of densities, and random features. Benchmark results demonstrate advantages of the approach. Its distinctive contribution is jointly modeling where observations occur and what values they contain through interpretable, complementary factors.
icml-2022-nonparametric-sparse-tensor-fa.tldr: A nonparametric tensor model separates intrinsic properties from interaction activity while jointly modeling sparse observation patterns and nonlinear entry values.

paragraphs: Tracking an object becomes especially difficult when it disappears completely behind something else. The visible image no longer directly tells a model where the object is. This paper studies how representations can learn object permanence, meaning the ability to keep localizing objects through occlusion, without human annotations of invisible positions or assumptions about object dynamics.

The proposed learning signal rewards temporal coherence in memory. A sequence encoder produces features that incorporate information from the sequence, and the method fits a Markov walk over a graph linking memories across space and time. Although the walk is Markovian, its states are features with memory of the sequence, allowing past information to participate in the learning objective.

Optimizing this objective produces a memory representation that retains occluded objects and predicts their motion to improve localization. On several datasets of increasing complexity and realism, the model outperforms existing approaches with minimal supervision. The findings show that object permanence can emerge from organizing memory consistently over time, without directly labeling the locations of objects while they are hidden.
icml-2022-object-permanence-emerges-in-a.tldr: A self-supervised memory-coherence objective learns to localize occluded objects without annotations of hidden locations or assumptions about their dynamics.

paragraphs: Pairwise Conditional Gradients extends the Frank–Wolfe algorithm and is attractive when a solution should use few components. However, it can take swap steps that fail to make sufficient progress on the objective. Existing bounds on the number of such steps depend on dimension, preventing those guarantees from extending directly to infinite-dimensional problems such as kernel herding.

The proposed Blended Pairwise Conditional Gradients algorithm removes swap steps entirely. It is designed to be easy to implement and needs no internal gradient alignment procedure. Its convergence rate essentially matches the comparison rate for Pairwise Conditional Gradients without drop steps, giving guarantees that are no worse and improving or establishing rates in multiple cases.

Numerical experiments also find substantially sparser solutions than those produced by the original pairwise method. The authors apply the algorithm to kernel herding, deriving quadrature rules and demonstrating performance numerically. The work therefore addresses both a theoretical obstacle caused by dimension-dependent step counts and the practical goal of representing solutions with fewer components.
icml-2022-pairwise-conditional-gradients.tldr: Blended Pairwise Conditional Gradients removes problematic swap steps, strengthens convergence guarantees, and produces sparser solutions in experiments.

paragraphs: Variational methods approximate a target distribution using a family of distributions that can be optimized. Earlier work developed a path-gradient estimator for simple Gaussian approximations and argued that it is particularly useful when the approximation gets close to the exact target. That creates a mismatch in many applications: a simple Gaussian may be unable to reach the regime where the estimator is most beneficial.

This paper extends path-gradient estimation to continuous normalizing flows, a substantially more expressive variational family. The change broadens the distributions that can be represented while retaining the path-gradient approach to optimization. It addresses the representational restriction of the earlier setting, making the estimator applicable beyond simple Gaussian approximations.

The authors describe an efficient algorithm for computing the new estimator and demonstrate superior performance empirically. The contribution joins two aspects of variational learning: the flexibility of the approximating family and the way optimization gradients are estimated. A richer family provides greater scope to approach the target distribution, where prior work motivated the usefulness of path gradients.
icml-2022-path-gradient-estimators-for-c.tldr: Path-gradient estimation is extended from simple Gaussian approximations to continuous normalizing flows, with efficient computation and empirical performance gains.

paragraphs: Neural classifiers are often designed around one particular relationship between concepts. A hierarchical classifier organizes concepts through a hierarchy, while a fairness-oriented classifier may seek to shield a protected field. Once a specialized architecture is chosen, changing the kind of relationship it should express can be difficult. This paper proposes a shared architecture for a broader range of relationships.

The concept subspace network, or CSN, generalizes existing specialized classifiers into a model that can learn multiple kinds of concept relationships. Its design draws on prototype-based classifiers that promote interpretability. The goal is to make the organization of concepts adjustable within one modeling framework, rather than tying the architecture to a single classification objective.

The authors demonstrate state-of-the-art fairness results when concept independence is enforced. They also show that CSNs can be transformed into hierarchical classifiers and can reconcile fairness and hierarchy within one classifier. Performance matches that of the prototype-based models inspiring the design. These findings support a unified approach to classification tasks whose concept relationships would otherwise motivate separate specialized architectures.
icml-2022-prototype-based-classification.tldr: Concept subspace networks unify prototype-based classification across fairness, hierarchy, and combinations of those concept relationships.

paragraphs: Linear Symmetry-Based Disentanglement, or LSBD, gives a formal meaning to representations whose disentangled structure is described through linear symmetries. A definition alone does not provide a practical way to measure whether a learned representation meets it. This paper introduces D_LSBD to fill that evaluation gap and connect LSBD with earlier notions of disentanglement.

The authors provide a mathematically grounded metric and a practical implementation for SO(2) groups. They then derive LSBD-VAE from the metric, turning the evaluation principle into a semi-supervised learning method. This links the property being measured to the objective used to learn representations, with limited supervision supplied about transformations.

Their evaluations find that common VAE-based disentanglement methods do not learn LSBD representations in the studied cases. LSBD-VAE and other recent methods can learn them with limited transformation supervision. The resulting representations also achieve several desirable properties captured by existing disentanglement metrics. The findings distinguish the symmetry-based criterion from conventional evaluations while showing that satisfying it can coexist with other useful notions of disentanglement.
icml-2022-quantifying-and-learning-linea.tldr: A new metric measures linear symmetry-based disentanglement and yields a semi-supervised VAE that can learn representations satisfying it.

paragraphs: Models of human auditory processing have often used manually designed acoustic filters or representations learned by supervised audio networks. This paper asks whether self-supervised speech models provide better representations for predicting brain responses to speech. It evaluates features from APC, wav2vec, wav2vec 2.0, and HuBERT against fMRI recordings in the auditory cortex.

Across the comparisons, representations from the middle layers of these self-supervised models give the best prediction performance relative to acoustic baselines, phonemic features, and supervised models. The relationship also varies across brain regions: areas associated with lower-level auditory processing prefer earlier model layers, while areas involved in higher-level semantic processing prefer later ones.

The authors connect this pattern to the information represented at different depths, including acoustic, phonetic, and lexical information. Model depth thus provides representations relevant to different stages of cortical speech processing. The results establish strong predictive models of auditory responses and support a correspondence between representational hierarchies in self-supervised speech networks and the hierarchy of information used across human cortical regions.
icml-2022-self-supervised-models-of-audi.tldr: Self-supervised speech representations predict auditory-cortex responses well, with layer depth corresponding to different levels of speech processing.

paragraphs: A predictor’s performance across an entire population is only one way to assess it. Multi-group agnostic learning instead focuses on conditional risks: the prediction risk within particular subgroups of that population. This makes subgroup performance an explicit part of the learning criterion, connecting the mathematical problem to concerns about subgroup fairness and hidden stratification.

The paper studies the structure of solutions to this multi-group problem. The central question is what it means to solve a learning task when performance is considered within groups, rather than only through a population-wide quantity. Examining solution structure provides a theoretical account of the objects that an algorithm for this criterion should seek.

The authors then provide algorithms described as both simple and near-optimal for the learning problem. Their contribution combines an analysis of the criterion’s solutions with procedures for learning under it. For applications concerned with subgroup performance, the significance is that these concerns are treated as a formal learning objective with algorithmic support, giving a principled basis for considering risks within a population.
icml-2022-simple-and-near-optimal-algori.tldr: The paper analyzes multi-group learning solutions and supplies simple, near-optimal algorithms for a criterion focused on subgroup risks.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to represent uncertainty about what a model has learned, which can help when test inputs differ from training inputs. Placing uncertainty over network weights can be computationally expensive. Node-based alternatives instead learn fixed weight estimates and multiply hidden nodes by latent random variables, providing a more scalable source of epistemic uncertainty.

This paper interprets those random variables as implicitly applying simple, domain-agnostic perturbations to training data. From that perspective, node randomness helps explain performance when covariate shift comes from corrupted inputs. The authors observe that the diversity of these implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables, and propose increasing that entropy during training.

Evaluations on out-of-distribution image classification benchmarks show improved uncertainty estimation for node-based Bayesian networks under input perturbations. The method also provides robustness to noisy training labels as a side effect. The work connects an internal probabilistic mechanism to a concrete data-perturbation interpretation, then uses that interpretation to motivate a straightforward change to training.
icml-2022-tackling-covariate-shift-with-.tldr: Increasing latent-node entropy improves uncertainty estimation under input corruption by diversifying implicit training perturbations in Bayesian neural networks.
